analysis.title: Multi-asset market outlook, November 2026: Rhapsody in blue for stock pickers after Democratic sweep of US midterm elections
key_insights: Democrats won both houses of Congress in the midterms. The president keeps a veto, so the Democratic agenda is hard to pass, but they could limit fiscal expansion, and the looming debt ceiling adds risk. Robeco expects Republicans to eventually agree a deal to protect their 2028 presidential chances.

The main new risk is state-level data-center pauses, especially in Texas and Kansas, where new projects may face stricter controls on energy and water use. Investors initially read it as negative for semiconductors and AI infrastructure, speeding up deleveraging seen in recent weeks.
Equity markets are treating the midterm result as a clearing event. History suggests equities perform well when Congress and the president are from different parties.

Diversification away from the narrow AI focus is expected to create a stock picker's market as dispersion broadens. A slower cloud buildout weakens the AI adoption trade, but broader economic momentum should support the recent rotation.
Credit spreads are the bellwether for financing the AI buildout. A slower buildout eases near-term capital raising needs, but delayed revenue realization increases pressure on business models.

Robeco's 50:50 multi-asset portfolios stay long global equities, favoring the US on strong earnings and the AI theme. They increased hedging in Europe, moving high-yield hedging from the US to Europe on a more vulnerable Eurozone debt market.

Robeco added to US dollar holdings, funded by selling euros, as rate differentials compressed. It believes European rate expectations are too high given economic headwinds and French political and debt risk.
Robeco remains cautious on oil because it cannot predict whether a 'deal' will reopen the Strait of Hormuz and secure Gulf energy exports.

October performance: energy prices surged and drove broad commodity gains. Fixed income recovered broadly despite inflation fears from oil and labor costs. EM equities sold off sharply on tech supply chain weakness, regulatory scrutiny and political risk. DM equities were flat. Gold fell on liquidity demands and rising real yields. Global real estate rebounded.
Global growth is robust. JP Morgan global manufacturing PMI was 52.6 in October, and South Korean exports have not rolled over, which Robeco reads as room for the expansion to run.

China's September exports accelerated to 36.3% y/y and the trade surplus widened, reducing pressure for fiscal stimulus. China's official PMI fell to 49.3 (contraction) while the private, export-oriented PMI was 52.0.

The Fed held in October and signaled tighter conditions since September. Robeco says a December hike seems on the cards. Payrolls rose 165,000 but wage growth fell 10 bps to 3.1%, so the labor market is not materially tightening.

US unemployment fell to 4.1%, but 339,000 more people worked part-time for economic reasons. Nominal wage growth near 3% against nominal GDP growth above 6% keeps labor costs supportive of the profit cycle.

Earnings are the swing factor. Resilient earnings could broaden capex beyond the AI ecosystem, and the recent drop in real yields is a tailwind. The cycle risk is a financial conditions tightening and narrower earnings breadth stalling AI capex.

A large US equity sell-off would hit consumers disproportionately because consumption relies on the wealth effect over income. Another Middle East flare-up could cap real wage growth and hurt lower-income spending.
